analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau, 16.0% of construction firms reported using AI in the most recent survey period, up from 14.3% in the prior period. This represents direct measurement from the Census BTOS series, which asks firms fortnightly whether they have used AI in the preceding two weeks. The uptick suggests gradual but measurable adoption across the sector, though three-quarters of construction firms still report no AI use in any given two-week window.

BuiltWorlds, the sector intelligence network, documents that construction technology research increasingly centers on applied AI and machine learning across the architecture, engineering, and construction workflow. The organization tracks adoption patterns in site robotics, jobsite IoT systems, and digital preconstruction tools, and hosts an annual AI/ML Conference focused on the expanding role of these technologies throughout the construction, building, and operation process. That conference framework—examining implementation strategies at both project and enterprise levels alongside documented case studies—suggests vendors and integrators are moving beyond pilot stages toward systematic deployment.

The Associated General Contractors of America, representing over 27,000 member firms, has positioned technology adoption tracking as part of its core industry surveillance. AGC surveys contractor adoption of technology and safety-technology compliance across US builders, establishing the trade body as the primary source for adoption records within the general contracting segment. While the sourced materials do not detail specific AI use cases from AGC data, the organization's scope indicates that safety monitoring and operational compliance tools are embedded in its tracking agenda.

The source materials do not provide evidence of measured ROI, vendor concentration, specific deployment targets, or regulatory posture for construction AI. The excerpts indicate that research and convening infrastructure exists around construction AI, but do not quantify returns, market share, risk assessments, or compliance requirements that would inform deployment decisions. Firms considering AI adoption in construction should rely on the documented Census figure as an adoption baseline and on direct engagement with sector conferences and peer benchmarking programs to assess use-case fit and returns, rather than looking to published sector research for those details at this time.

https://cretech.com/.brief: According to the page, CREtech New York 2026 will be held at the Javits Center in New York City on October 20, 21, 2026, and will bring together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. The event is described as a leading real-estate AI conference where sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI in their portfolios, offering real strategy rather than theory. The conference aims to connect owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction firms, brokers, and tech leaders to discuss AI’s impact on real-estate assets. Tickets are limited, and sponsors and partners are said to represent companies shaping the future of real-estate in the age of AI.

https://www.agc.org/.brief: AGC’s Leadership for Project Executives Course (LPEC) trains new project executives to handle high-impact responsibilities. The organization offers a single platform that guides projects from initial estimate to final report, and it serves more than 27,000 member firms with services that aim to improve construction quality and protect the public interest. An Association Survey reported that construction input costs rose 8.9% from August 2025 to August 2026, citing war and tariff impacts, and that contractors added 22,000 jobs in August while the construction unemployment rate fell to a record low of 3.1%, yet firms still struggle to fill openings. Another survey found that workforce shortages in construction remain acute even in a soft market, with data centers further straining labor supply.

https://builtworlds.com/.brief: BuiltWorlds operates a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals. The organization hosts an annual Buildings Conference addressing innovation in building development, design, materials and systems, with particular focus on data centers and AI infrastructure. It also runs an annual AI/ML Conference exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning adoption across the architecture, engineering, construction and operations industry, covering implementation strategies, use cases, and lessons learned from companies deploying these technologies.
